kp.k: Harvey's growth does not establish lasting market dominance
kp.d: Abramowitz describes Harvey reaching a five billion valuation in under three years and attracting leading firms and legal departments. Waters regards its growth as remarkable but rejects vendor-centric 'winning' narratives and expects continued competition among horizontal AI platforms, with substantial market share still available. These are the speakers' market assessments, not independently documented findings in the transcript.
qs: In under three years, they have gone from a stealth partnership with OpenAI and then eventually Alan and Ovary, to a five billion, that's a billion with a B, valuation
I personally don't like to talk about winning in terms of particular vendors.
There's still a lot of market share for grabs, but the industry is exploding in terms of AI and gen AI offerings.

kp.k: Prestigious partnerships helped overcome startup procurement concerns
kp.d: Waters says early partnerships with major legal organisations increased confidence in Harvey. From observing UK and European announcements, she interpreted its selection of leading local firms as a strategy to recruit credible partners able and willing to invest in the relationship. She distinguishes that perceived strategy from the initial waitlist, which she attributes to a small product-focused team lacking sales capacity rather than deliberate exclusivity marketing.
qs: That was a very small team focused on building out the product and not actually having a proper sales and GTM organization to deal with the immediate inflow of inquiries that they got.
picking off typically, the number one or number two player, local player in that jurisdiction.
they were getting someone credible in that market, that they knew we're going to be able to invest and be willing to invest in them and in that relationship.

kp.k: Data security initially mattered more than legal specialisation
kp.d: For the second half of 2023, Waters describes the primary adoption driver as being able to reassure clients about data handling, security architecture and geographic residency, especially for a UK-headquartered global firm. The initial proposition was a safer ChatGPT-like experience rather than demonstrated superiority over ChatGPT. She links the same concern to firms building chatbots within Azure.
qs: the concern was less a legal specific product, but a product that law firms in particular could hold their hands up to their clients and say, I have a lot more comfort about what's happening with your data.
You always wanted the safe ChatGPT, which is why we saw so many law firms start to build their own chat bots in the Azure infrastructure
Not I'm going to be a product that beats ChatGPT, but actually, I can say something about the security of the architecture.

kp.k: Ashurst's selection reflected timing, availability and global coverage
kp.d: Waters reports initial Harvey conversations in mid-summer 2023, trials in autumn 2023 and full enterprise rollout in June 2024, with substantial product development during that interval. She explicitly says the trials were not head-to-head comparisons: Harvey was the main legal option in their consideration, alongside Copilot and a domain-specific tool. Co-Counsel was not offering them a trial or an international roadmap at that stage; by 2024, Ashurst's investment thinking had already advanced. The account therefore does not establish comparative product superiority.
qs: between my first conversation, which was mid-summer 2023 until Ashurst actually did the full enterprise rollout, which was June 2024, the product had evolved immensely just in that short time period.
what we did was we didn't do any head-to-heads
Co-Council was not yet offering us a trial, because we were doing that in the autumn of, the Northern Hemisphere, autumn of 2023.
they didn't have an international road map.

kp.d: Waters identifies a feature available during the autumn 2023 trial that generated an issues list from an uploaded redline or blackline document. For transactional lawyers, this mapped directly onto identifying contract changes and preparing client discussions and negotiations. She reports audible gasps during a rollout demonstration, evidence of perceived usefulness and enthusiasm rather than measured accuracy or productivity gains.

So that's how lawyers work when you're dealing with contracts between versions and changes is to identify all the changes, and start creating lists of all the changes, and then what you need to talk to your client about, what you need to negotiate.
there was one session in particular, there was audible gasps in the audience.

kp.k: Practical use tempers replacement fears and demands user learning
kp.d: Drawing on later pilots at other firms, Waters describes lawyers moving from excitement and job anxiety to recognising that the tools require effort and cannot take over a person's job. Effective adoption involves learning suitable tasks and how to interact with the system. She warns against using general legal AI products for legal research unless they are actual legal research tools, and says users often ignore that warning.
qs: this isn't magic and this isn't ready to go take over a person's job.
they realize it's a bit of hard yards for them to actually use it really well.
please don't use it to do your legal research, unless it's an actual legal research tool
But now I'm learning and I'm understanding a little bit better how I interface with it in order to get the most out of it.

kp.d: Abramowitz reports a Law 360 survey published earlier that year showing lawyer AI use rising over the preceding year from 'like 35% to 55%', greater liking among users and no perceived threat to billable hours. No sample size or methodological details are supplied. His suggestion that lawyers might be right about billable hours is an interpretation, not evidence that AI has no effect on hours or pricing.

kp.k: AI currently absorbs excess workload rather than freeing lawyers
kp.d: Waters's practitioner observation is that overloaded lawyers use generative AI to complete work they otherwise would not reach, rather than suddenly gaining free time. She extends this beyond legal tasks to senior responsibilities such as business development, training, team management and governance. Abramowitz supports the interpretation with his experience of unfinished transactional workloads. This is an anecdotal account of capacity expansion, not a quantified labour-market finding.
qs: the ability to have access to GenAI, whether it's just an assistant or some other type, is ultimately just letting them get through their day, do work that they just would never get to
I think right now the AI is helping us get through more of that. But that doesn't mean that actually we're getting through it all.
whether it's BD, training, managing the team, working on governance, thinking about performance, all of that.

kp.k: Agentic substitution remains immature in the speakers' assessment
kp.d: Abramowitz reports Andrei Karpathy's view that 2025 might begin a decade of agents rather than be the year of agents, interpreting this as support for longer-lasting human–AI assistance. Waters agrees that agent hype is premature and says the features and products she sees need greater maturity before substantially changing work. These are expectations and experience-based assessments, not established deployment forecasts.

I think the hype around the agents is a little early
I think that maturity level, it still needs to come up the curve to be something that truly shifts the way people are doing work.

kp.k: Workflow automation may preserve inefficient ways of working
kp.d: Waters distinguishes speeding up existing legal processes from redesigning how work is done. She would like agents with access to lawyers' tools to discover different, better methods rather than reproduce current checklists, but says she has not yet seen systems taking that direction. Her argument is a recommendation for transformation, not a claim that such autonomous redesign is already available.

to actually find a different and better way to get the work done, then the step-by-step that I have in my mind and the checklist that I have in my mind.
I don't think yet I'm seeing anything that's taking us on that path.

kp.d: Abramowitz asks whether rising lawyers might prefer founding AI-native firms to pursuing partnership, and whether AI-native corporate clients might choose those providers over established firms. He frames this as a business-model question that matters more than vendor selection. The transcript presents these as possible future competitive developments, not observed departures or demonstrated shifts in client purchasing.

kp.k: Long-term redesign could challenge pyramids and reshape lawyer development
kp.d: Waters calls the industry an 'evolutionary disruption event' and recommends leadership define desired client and employee experiences over 10, 20 or 30 years, then work backwards rather than begin with tools or existing structures. Her hypothetical includes abandoning the staffing pyramid and enabling individuals to multiply productivity and value by 10 to 50X. She stresses training, experience, expertise and external relationships alongside technology, and acknowledges that the technological seeds she sees are far from that vision. The multipliers are aspirational scenario assumptions, not measured results.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: Tara Waters describes near-term augmentation of lawyers, continuing competition among legal-AI vendors, and a longer-term possibility of fundamental organizational change.
pts.d: Waters expects legal AI to remain highly competitive rather than treating Harvey as a definitive winner. She attributes some of Harvey's credibility to its partnerships with leading local firms and reports substantial product development between Ashurst's initial discussions and enterprise rollout. She says early adoption was driven principally by data security and regional data protection requirements, not demonstrated superiority to ChatGPT. As a concrete change to transactional work, she describes Harvey generating an issues list from an existing redline or blackline document. From subsequent pilots, she reports that lawyers discover these tools require effort and are not ready to replace a person's job. Her present-tense account is that AI helps overloaded lawyers complete more work, including work previously left undone, rather than necessarily creating free time. She considers agentic features immature and distinguishes speeding up existing processes from finding better ways to perform legal work. Longer term, she characterizes the industry as undergoing evolutionary disruption and proposes imagining organizations in which individuals deliver 10–50 times their productivity and value, potentially making the existing staffing pyramid unnecessary. Those multipliers and structural changes are an envisioned direction, not measured outcomes or a firm forecast.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: Waters primarily relies on firsthand implementation and consulting experience, observed product capabilities, and qualitative lawyer feedback; her transformative scenarios are speculative.
pts.d: For Harvey's market position, Waters draws on observing partnerships with prominent firms across UK and European jurisdictions and interpreting that selection as a strategy to secure credible partners able to invest in the relationship. For product development and usability, she draws on leading Ashurst's evaluation and rollout, including demonstrations of issues-list generation and lawyers' reactions. She explicitly says Ashurst did not conduct head-to-head comparisons among competing legal-specific products; the options considered were constrained by availability and international suitability. For augmentation and workload claims, she cites experience running pilots at another firm and reports from lawyers that AI enables previously neglected work. For agent maturity, she offers her assessment of features and products she has seen. Her 10–50X scenario is supported only by her perception of early technological possibilities, not quantitative productivity evidence. Waters provides no benchmark results, controlled productivity study, or measured job-displacement evidence in this interview. The host's survey figures and his quotation of another commentator are not treated as evidence supplied by Waters.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: Waters separates the 2023–2024 adoption experience and current tool limitations from organizational transformation envisioned over decades.
pts.d: The retrospective Harvey account spans initial conversations in mid-summer 2023, trials in autumn 2023, and Ashurst's full enterprise rollout in June 2024. Early procurement priorities and limited product choice belong to that period: Waters says Co-Counsel only became a viable option for them in 2024, after their first-investment thinking was advanced. Her claims about workload relief, the effort needed to use AI effectively, and immature agentic features describe conditions at the time of the 2025 interview, not permanent limits on AI. Effective use depends on learning what tools can and cannot do; she specifically warns against legal research using tools not designed for that purpose. She wants agents with access to workplace tools to find different and better methods, but says she has not yet seen that direction realized. Her proposed strategic horizons are 10, 20, and 30 years, with client and employee experience considered 20–30 years ahead. These are planning horizons, not promised delivery dates for 10–50X gains. Realizing that vision would require training, experience, relationships, and organizational redesign, not technology alone. She also rejects framing the vendor market as already won.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The claims principally concern large and global law firms, transactional lawyers, overloaded practitioners and senior lawyers, clients whose data is processed, and firm leadership considering future staffing and service models.
pts.d: Waters's adoption account is especially grounded in a large, UK-headquartered global firm operating across jurisdictions with complex data protection rules. Clients are affected through the handling and location of their data. Transactional lawyers across seniority levels are affected by automatic preparation of issues lists used to identify contractual changes, advise clients, and prepare negotiations. Lawyers more broadly face a learning burden but can use AI to manage excessive workloads. For senior lawyers, that workload includes business development, training, team management, governance, and performance responsibilities as well as legal matters. Vendors face continued competition, while credible firms able to invest in partnerships helped Harvey establish its market position. In Waters's longer-term scenario, firm leaders would reconsider client and employee experiences, the junior-heavy staffing pyramid, and how individuals develop expertise and external relationships while becoming more productive. She does not quantify changes in headcount, specify which roles would disappear, or claim access-to-justice outcomes.
